entries.name: Stratovolcano (composite volcano)
entries.era: still forming; many are active
entries.purpose: volcanic conduit venting molten rock and gas from the mantle to the surface
entries.found: ring of fire: Japan (Fuji, 3776 m), Cascades (Rainier, 4392 m), Andes, Aleutians, Vesuvius and Etna (Italy)
entries.notes: The classic cone. Alternating layers make flanks unstable; rare huge collapses (Unzen 1792, St. Helens 1980) reshape the mountain in minutes.

entries.name: Shield volcano
entries.era: still forming; active
entries.purpose: basaltic vent with very fluid lava that travels far and thins into a broad dome
layout: flank rifts aligned along weak zones
entries.found: Hawaii (Mauna Loa, summit 4169 m, edifice ~120 km across), Iceland, Galapagos
entries.notes: Width dwarfs height: Mauna Loa measures ~9 km from deep-sea base to summit. Eruptions are usually non-explosive but lavas can swallow whole districts.

entries.name: Cinder cone (scoria cone)
entries.era: still forming; often short-lived
entries.purpose: small volcano built of ballistic fragments from a single, sometimes monogenetic vent
layout: cone slope ~30 degrees at the angle of repose
entries.found: Paricutin (Mexico, grew from a cornfield 1943-1952, final height 424 m), Sunset Crater (Arizona, ~260 m), Eifel (Germany)
entries.notes: A cone can grow in months. Loose cinders crumble underfoot; solid core only near the vent.

entries.name: Lava dome (cryptodome)
entries.era: still forming; episodically active
entries.purpose: bulbous mound of viscous lava squeezed out of a vent like toothpaste
parts: talus apron of broken dome rock
layout: rounded steep-sided mound in a vent or crater
entries.found: Mount St. Helens (1980-86 dacite dome), Novarupta dome (Alaska, 1912), Montserrat (Soufriere Hills, 1995-now)
entries.notes: Domes overgrow their strength and collapse, making lethal block-and-ash flows. Watch them after big eruptions.

entries.name: Volcanic caldera
entries.era: still forming; Yellowstone and similar stay active for 10^5 years
entries.purpose: collapse depression left when an emptied magma chamber can no longer support the roof
layout: enclosed basin, often with a lake
rim lower and broader than a stratovolcano rim
entries.found: Crater Lake (Oregon, 8 x 10 km, 594 m deep), Yellowstone (USA, ~70 x 45 km), Tambora (Indonesia), Santorini (Greece)
entries.notes: A structure at the largest scale a volcano can make: eruption empties a chamber, the roof sags in. All that remains above is the rim and a very deep lake.

entries.name: Waterfall
entries.era: still forming; retreats upstream over time
entries.purpose: knickpoint where a river crosses a rock layer harder than the one below it
layout: gorge eroded upstream of the lip over centuries
entries.found: Niagara Falls (~51 m), Victoria Falls (108 m high, 1.7 km wide), Angel Falls (Venezuela, 979 m), Gullfoss (Iceland)
entries.notes: Typical faces are only a few metres high; notes carry the extremes. Water undercuts the lip, so the whole feature migrates upstream. Victoria Falls is the widest single curtain of falling water on Earth.

entries.name: Canyon / gorge
entries.era: still forming; downcut by river over 10^6 years
entries.purpose: incision where a river cuts through hard rock faster than slopes can fill the gap
layout: river at the bottom or dry wash
entries.found: Grand Canyon (Colorado River, 446 km long, ~29 km wide, depth ~1.6 km), Kali Gandaki (Nepal), Blyde River Canyon (South Africa), slot canyons of the Utah deserts (Antelope Canyon, metres wide)
entries.notes: Two archetypes: deep open canyons (Grand Canyon) and narrow slot canyons cut in sandstone. Slot canyons flash-flood with little warning upstream.

entries.name: Natural arch
entries.era: still forming; eroded over 10^4-10^5 years
entries.purpose: residual bridge left when weathering punches through a fin of rock but not through its legs
layout: fin-like wall pierced by an opening
one or more arches stacked vertically
entries.found: Arches National Park, USA (over 2,000 recorded arches); Landscape Arch (span ~88 m); Delicate Arch (freestanding, ~16 m tall); natural bridges of Utah and Kentucky (Natural Bridge State Resort Park)
entries.notes: Arches are ephemeral on geological time: Landscape Arch lost a slab in 1991. Expect a landmark to change or vanish during a long game.

entries.name: Mesa
entries.era: still forming; eroded over 10^6-10^7 years
entries.purpose: remnant plateau: caprock-protected tableland above eroded badland terrain
layout: cliff walls above slope-washed lower slopes
entries.found: Monument Valley (Arizona/Utah, buttes and mesas up to ~300 m), Chaco Canyon edges, the Altiplano of Bolivia and Peru, Ethiopian Highlands
entries.notes: Flat tops are the survivors of a once-continuous plateau; mesas shrink to buttes then to pinnacles. Caprock hardness is everything.

entries.name: Butte / pinnacle
entries.era: still forming; eroded over 10^6-10^7 years
entries.purpose: late-stage remnant of a mesa: a steep isolated hill of caprock-capped strata
layout: often one of several in a valley of remnants
entries.found: Monument Valley (East and West Mitten Buttes, Merrick Butte), the Pawnee Buttes (Colorado), Kaibab edges (Arizona)
entries.notes: The final stage before a butte erodes away. A row of buttes marks the line of an ancient plateau escarpment.

entries.name: Sea stack
entries.era: still forming; one collapse per sea arch per century
entries.purpose: isolated pillar left when a sea arch roof collapses; the last stage of headland erosion
parts: boulder beach and reef around the base
layout: isolated pillar offshore from a headland
entries.found: Old Harry Rocks (Dorset, chalk), stack group at Hvitserkur (Iceland), Héligoland (Germany), Puffin Island stacks (Wales), the needles of Crete and the Hebrides
entries.notes: The erosion sequence headland -> cave -> arch -> stack -> stump is legible from a boat. Nesting seabirds (puffins, guillemots) crowd the tops.

entries.name: Limestone cave (solution cave)
entries.era: still forming; 10^5-10^7 years of dissolution
entries.purpose: dissolution void following joints in soluble bedrock, drained or flooded by groundwater
layout: horizontal or inclined solution passages following joints
entries.found: Mammoth Cave, USA (more than 600 km of surveyed passages, world's longest known system), Carlsbad Caverns, the Skocjan and Postojna caves (Slovenia), Sistema Sac Actun (Mexico)
entries.notes: Dark, constant-temperature habitat for troglobites (blind white fish, cave crickets) and shelter for hibernating bats. Entrances were among the earliest human shelters.

entries.name: Sand dune (barchan / transverse / star)
entries.era: still forming; migrates with prevailing wind
entries.purpose: aeolian accumulation where sand is trapped downwind of an obstacle
parts: leeward slip face (angle of repose ~32 deg)
layout: transverse: straight ridges perpendicular to wind
entries.found: Namib Desert (star dunes up to ~300 m), Simpson Desert (Australia, barchans), Gobi, Sahara ergs, coastal dunes of Oregon and Curonian Spit (Lithuania)
entries.notes: Dunes migrate metres per year; horns advance faster than centres. Slip faces avalanche constantly, burying tracks and camps.

entries.name: Valley glacier
entries.era: still forming; most are retreating now
entries.purpose: permanent river of ice moving downhill under gravity and its own weight
layout: long tongue of ice flowing from a cirque or icefield
meltwater river emerges at the snout
entries.found: Franz Josef and Fox glaciers (New Zealand, reach sea-level rainforest), Alps (Aletsch, 22 km long), Patagonia (Southern Patagonian Ice Field), Jakobshavn (Greenland, fastest in the world at over 40 m/day peak flow)
entries.notes: River-like flow: ice deforms and slides on meltwater. Crevasse zones are deadly; the snout retreats visibly year by year in most climates.

entries.name: Fjord
entries.era: still forming; carved in ice ages, drowned by rising seas
entries.purpose: drowned glacial trough: a U-shaped valley flooded by post-glacial sea rise
layout: sill at the mouth, overdeepened inside
entries.found: Norway (Sognefjord, 204 km long, 1308 m max depth, walls over 1 km), Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound (New Zealand), Scoresby Sund (Greenland), Puget Sound (USA)
entries.notes: Deeper inside than at the mouth because ice carved the basin below sea level. Near-vertical walls with waterfalls are the game-ready silhouette.

entries.name: Tower karst (fengcong / fenglin)
entries.era: still forming; 10^6-10^7 years of dissolution
entries.purpose: extreme residual karst: isolated limestone towers left by tropical dissolution
parts: alluvial plain or sea between towers
layout: clusters of towers separated by flat plain (fengcong)
isolated towers in open water or fields (fenglin)
entries.found: Guilin and Yangshuo (China, towers typically 50-150 m), Ha Long Bay (Vietnam, ~1,600-2,000 islands), Khammouane and Vang Vieng (Laos), Phong Nha-Ke Bang
entries.notes: Karst needs limestone plus heavy rainfall. Ha Long's towers rise straight out of the Gulf of Tonkin; the same silhouette on land reads as Guilin. Caves perforate most towers.

entries.name: Coral reef (fringing / barrier)
entries.era: still forming; reefs grow over thousands of years
entries.purpose: biogenic breakwater: living coral builds a limestone framework that shelters shallow lagoons
parts: reef crest (often exposed at low tide)
back-reef lagoon with patches and sand
layout: line or arc of reef parallel to shore (fringing) or offshore (barrier)
lagoon of calm shallow water behind the crest
entries.found: Great Barrier Reef (Australia, ~2,300 km long, ~2,900 individual reefs), Red Sea reefs, Caribbean reefs, Apo Reef (Philippines)
entries.notes: Less than 1% of the ocean floor but roughly a quarter of marine species live there. Needs warm (over ~18 C), clear, shallow water.

entries.name: Atoll
entries.era: still forming; subsidence of a volcanic island over 10^6-10^7 years
materials: black lava rock (only on volcanic atolls)
entries.purpose: ring of coral reef and low islets around the site of a sunken volcano
layout: closed or broken ring of islets
shallow lagoon inside, often 20-60 m deep
ocean on the outside drops off steeply
entries.found: Tuamotu Archipelago (French Polynesia), the Maldives, Kwajalein (Marshall Islands, ~120 km across, among the largest), Funafuti (Tuvalu)
entries.notes: Darwin's subsidence theory: fringing reef -> barrier reef -> atoll as the island sinks. Highest point rarely exceeds 3-4 m above sea level.

entries.name: River delta
entries.era: still forming; built over centuries to millennia
entries.purpose: deposition where a river drops its sediment load entering still water
entries.found: Nile (arcuate, ~240 km across), Mississippi (bird-foot, ~29,000 sq km including old lobes), Danube (~4,300 sq km), Mekong (~40,000 sq km), Sundarbans (Ganges-Brahmaputra)
entries.notes: Flat, fertile and flood-prone. Distributaries bifurcate endlessly; the coastline advances year by year. Home to some of the densest human populations.

entries.name: Oasis (spring-fed)
entries.era: still forming; fed by groundwater that may be thousands of years old
entries.purpose: reliable water point where groundwater reaches the surface in arid land
layout: concentric rings of denser vegetation outward
channels carry water to fields in tended oases
entries.found: Siwa (Egypt), Huacachina (Peru, on a dune field), the oases of the Algerian Sahara (Timimoun), Ica oasis (Peru), Cold Desert oases of Central Asia (one of the most densely farmed regions on Earth per hectare)
entries.notes: An oasis is an ecological island: migrant birds, endemic species and trade routes all concentrate on it. Many rely on deep fossil aquifers that do not refill.

entries.name: Hot spring (thermal spring)
entries.era: still forming; may last millennia while heat flow continues
entries.purpose: surface expression of geothermal heat: groundwater heated by magma or deep circulation
parts: colored bacterial mats (up to ~100 C at the margin)
steam or vapor halo (milky thermal pools)
entries.found: Iceland (Reykjadalur steam river), Yellowstone (Mammoth Hot Springs, Grand Prismatic Spring ~90 m wide), Pamukkale fringe springs, Rotorua (New Zealand), Hierve el Agua (Mexico)
entries.notes: Thermophilic bacteria paint terraces in oranges and greens. Water can exceed 90 C; deaths at fenceless hot springs are real. Color rings map the temperature.

entries.name: Geyser
entries.era: still forming; erupts on a cycle of minutes to years
entries.purpose: violent hydrothermal vent: superheated water flash-boils and ejects itself upward
layout: narrow vent at or near ground level
for many geysers a pool is the visible part
entries.found: Yellowstone (Old Faithful, eruptions 32-56 m, every 44-110 min; Steamboat, the world's tallest active geyser, eruptions over 90 m), Haukadalur (Iceland, the Great Geysir), El Tatio (Chile)
entries.notes: Needs heat, water and a constriction. Only ~1,000 geysers remain active worldwide, about half in Yellowstone. Eruption height is stored pressure released at once.

entries.name: Chalk cliff
entries.era: still forming; undercut by the sea over 10^4 years
entries.purpose: vertical coastal escarpment of soft marine chalk, the classic white cliff
parts: talus of flint and chalk rubble
layout: long near-vertical wall following the coastline
entries.found: Dover and the White Cliffs of Albion (up to ~110 m), Seven Sisters (Sussex), Cap Blanc-Nez and Cap Gris-Nez (France), the chalk cliffs of Rugen and Mons Klint (Denmark)
entries.notes: Loose chalk sheds constant flakes and flints; whole faces calve off in rare storms. Flint in the wall tells the tide was here when the chalk was sea floor.

entries.name: Hoodoo (earth pyramid)
entries.era: still forming; eroded over 10^5-10^6 years
entries.purpose: eroded spire protected by a hard cap rock that resists weathering longer than its pedestal
layout: tallest spires under shelter of the Pink Cliffs escarpment
entries.found: Bryce Canyon National Park (Utah; typical hoodoos 1-15 m, largest ~45 m), the Walchia badland towers (Romania), Dolomites earth pyramids (Ritten, Italy)
entries.notes: Thin chemistry and frost do the work: rain dissolves soft strata, caprock shields the chimney. The Pink Cliffs' thousand spires are a canyon-wall stepped into a forest.

entries.name: Badlands (eroded waste terrain)
entries.era: still forming; gullied within decades of each storm
entries.purpose: dissected barren terrain where weak rock and flash rain make walking impossible
entries.found: Badlands National Park (South Dakota), Dinosaur Provincial Park (Alberta), Zabriskie Point (Death Valley), the eroded plateaus of Madagascar and Spain (Bardenas Reales)
entries.notes: Almost impassable off trail: slick after rain, dust-loose when dry. Gold and fossil fields - dinosaurs and mammoths turn up constantly.

entries.name: Travertine terraces (hot-spring cascades)
entries.era: still forming; rims grow millimetres per year
entries.purpose: stepped pools built as hot, carbonate-rich water cools and drops limestone
layout: staircase of pools descending a slope
white aprons widen as rims grow
entries.found: Pamukkale (Turkey; white cliff over the Denizli plain, UNESCO site, cotton-castle steps), Mammoth Hot Springs (Yellowstone), Huancavelica and Banos de Kanchuya (Peru), Hierve el Agua (Oaxaca)
entries.notes: Terraces are alive and regrow if water stops being blocked: fenced and un-fenced Pamukkale changed visibly in decades. Never climb the pools - boots crush the rims.

entries.name: Columnar basalt
entries.era: ancient; formed in fissure eruptions, still exposed by erosion
entries.purpose: regular polygonal jointing in cooling lava flows - nature's basalt columns
parts: curved columns where flow was directional
layout: steps where columns are exposed in section
entries.found: Giant's Causeway (Northern Ireland, approximately 40,000 columns, up to ~12 m tall), Devil's Postpile (California), Fingal's Cave (Scotland), Svartifoss (Iceland)
entries.notes: Hexagons are the most common cross-section (not the only). Fingal's Cave is a sea cave with hexagonal walls and an echo like wind in an organ pipe.

entries.name: Lava tube
entries.era: ancient; formed in eruptions, opened by later collapse
entries.purpose: drained conduit through which liquid lava once flowed below a solidified crust
entries.found: Kazumura Cave (Hawaii, about 65 km long, the world's longest and deepest known lava tube), Thurston Lava Tube (Hawaii Volcanoes NP), Sac Actun system shares limestone channel with lava-modified caves, Cueva del Viento (Tenerife)
entries.notes: Cold and dry inside, with fragile pāhoehoe floors. Hidden passages cross each other; surfaces above tubes can collapse into pits with no warning.

entries.name: Cenote (sinkhole lake)
entries.era: still forming; 10^5-10^6 years of roof collapse
entries.purpose: collapse sinkhole exposing a water-filled cave system in flat limestone plain
layout: circular shaft in a flat plain
entries.found: Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico (on the order of 10,000 cenotes, mostly aligned on the Ring of Cenotes), Ik Kil (about 60 m across, ~40 m deep), Sima de las Cotillas (Spain)
entries.notes: The Maya's only water source - temples and offerings lined the sacred cenotes. Visibility often 30+ m; diving requires cave certification.

entries.name: Inselberg (bornhardt)
entries.era: ancient; the surviving remnant of a vastly older mountain range
entries.purpose: isolated residual rock hill rising abruptly from a plain of deeply weathered and stripped regolith
layout: alone on a vast flat plain
sheer walls on one or more sides
entries.found: Uluru (arkose, rises 348 m above surrounding plain, total perimeter 9.4 km; strata 550-530 million years old), Kata Tjuta (The Olgas, ~36 domed bornhardts up to ~460 m above the plain), Sugarloaf Mountain (Rio de Janeiro), inselbergs of the Venezuelan Altiplano
entries.notes: Inselbergs are insel-mountains - 'islands of rock'. Most of Uluru's bulk lies underground; the Amadeus Basin sandstone extends far below.

entries.name: Tor (granite outcrop)
entries.era: ancient; corestones unroofed by erosion
entries.purpose: stacked free-standing granite corestones left after chemical weathering strips the joints
parts: often a shallow plateau remnant nearby
layout: usually on a ridge or moor top
entries.found: Dartmoor (Haytor, ~28 m high; more than 160 tors) and Bodmin Moor (UK), Bohemian Massif (Czechia), Bald Rock (NSW Australia, the largest unweathered granite tors)
entries.notes: Moorland tors are not quarried out - they are chemically weathered underground then uncovered. Easy climbing and 360-degree views make them Dartmoor's signature landmarks.

entries.name: Oxbow lake (meander cut-off)
entries.era: still forming; a meander cuts off in years to decades
entries.purpose: crescent-shaped lake left behind when a meander neck is breached in a flood
parts: crescent ridge of silt at the outer bend
layout: U-shaped arc paralleling the active channel
shallow and marshy at the tips
entries.found: Mississippi River (relicts like Horseshoe Lake, Arkansas), Amazon floodplain (countless oxbow lakes, many unnamed), Okavango Delta fringes, the meandering Dnieper and Danube plains
entries.notes: Some oxbows plug entirely and become backwater sloughs; the scenery itself records the river's path for thousands of years.

entries.name: Salt flat / dry lake (salar)
entries.era: still forming; seasonal flooding dissolves and redeposits the crust
entries.purpose: pan where enclosed drainage evaporates into a single, shimmering salt crust
layout: ridges of crust in polygonal patterns
mirror-like when wet, blindingly white when dry
entries.found: Salar de Uyuni (Bolivia, ~10,500 sq km, elevation 3,656 m, salt crust ~10 cm thick), Salar de Atacama (Chile), Bonneville Salt Flats (Utah), Lake Eyre (Australia, ephemeral), Qattara Depression (Egypt)
entries.notes: Blinding reflections and the world's flattest surface for GPS calibration; 10 cm of salt covers untold lithium and brine reserves. During the wet season it floods into a perfect mirror.

entries.name: Iceberg (tabular / growler)
entries.era: still forming; calving happens continuously, drift lasts years
entries.purpose: calved mass of glacier ice floating free in the ocean
parts: submerged keel (about 90% of mass is hidden)
layout: tabular: vast flat-topped slabs from ice shelves
non-tabular: jagged pinnacles from tidewater glaciers
growlers and bergy bits are small fragments
entries.found: Iceberg Alley (Newfoundland and the Grand Banks), Weddell Sea, the Drake Passage, the Gulf of St. Lawrence; Titanic sank after striking a moderate iceberg (~55 m tall, 120 m long)
entries.notes: An iceberg drafts 5-10x its freeboard height; tabular giants can exceed 100 m above water. Even small bergy bits can pierce steel hulls.

entries.name: Pingo (hydrolaccolith)
entries.era: still forming; grows over tens of thousands of years
entries.purpose: ice-cored hill forced upward as permafrost traps and freezes pressurised groundwater
parts: crater at the top once the cap ruptures
layout: solitary round dome on a flat tundra plain
often inside a drained lake basin (closed-system pingo)
entries.found: Mackenzie Delta, Canada (about 1,350 pingos, more than anywhere else), Ibyuk Pingo (~49 m, among the tallest known), Pingo National Landmark (Canada), North and Northeast Greenland
entries.notes: A pingo grows millimetres per year and takes millennia to reach maximum size. Top cap ruptures into a crater around the ice core - drone fetch material is pure ice.

entries.name: Esker
entries.era: ancient; deposited under ice sheets, exposed by their retreat
entries.purpose: sinuous ridge left by a meltwater river that ran inside a tunnel beneath a retreating glacier
parts: kettle holes where ice blocks melted
fine sand fans at the ends
layout: snake-like ridge winding across the plain
crest follows the buried tunnel path
gaps and sags where ice cores melted late
entries.found: Thelon Esker (Canada, several hundred km long), eskers of Finland and Scandinavia (often 10-30 m high and tens of km long), Munro Esker (Ontario), the 'kame' landscapes of Britain
entries.notes: Eskers are natural roadbeds in the taiga - flat dry gravel with clear 360-degree views. They ferry ancient drainage systems along the surface of the land.

entries.name: Maar (explosion crater)
entries.era: ancient; formed in a single violent steam explosion, often 10^4-10^5 years ago
entries.purpose: broad, shallow volcanic crater made when magma meets groundwater and blasts a pit
parts: often a lake filling the floor
layout: floor may be a circular lake
entries.found: Eifel maars (Germany; Laacher See is the best preserved, but most Eifel maars filled with water), Auvergne maars (France), Nyos and Monoun (Cameroon; their CO2-charged lakes killed thousands in 1986 and 1984), Kimberley diatreme field (South Africa)
entries.notes: Monogenetic: a single explosive eruption and done. Cold maar lakes stratify and store CO2 - Nyos and Monoun hold dissolved CO2 that burst in deadly clouds. Some maars sit above diamond-bearing diatremes.

entries.name: Glacial erratic
entries.era: ancient; deposited when glaciers retreated 10^4 years ago
materials: any bedrock foreign to the local geology
entries.purpose: stranded boulder carried by glacial ice and dropped when the ice melted
parts: often ice-gouged striae on the sides
sometimes perched in absurd positions (on roofs, on other rocks)
layout: alone on a flat plain or perched on bedrock
boulder either matches glacier flow direction or looks wildly out of place
entries.found: Okotoks Erratic (Alberta, Canada; over 16,000 tonnes), erratics of the Scottish coast (Saxa Vord etc.), Dover's flint erratics from Scandinavia, glacial erratics of the Baltic and Siberia, Chaos Ulear (Patagonia)
entries.notes: A misplaced block of bedrock miles from any outcrop of that type. Arranging the itinerary: an erratic's path is a glacier's fingerprint, and its setting tells its transport story.
